rv.q: In the end, it all comes down to Kate.
I only wish I could figure out who was reeling me in.
The three generate genuine sexual chemistry, further amplified by the cosmically grandiose décor.
Theater Company‘s Broadway revival of "Old Times" can’t possibly miss.
Initially the actors appear more interested in posing than in acting, but eventually they form a true ensemble.
Applying such attention-getting overstatement to an artist of the unspoken like Pinter sounds a trifle misguided.
Its fascination is quieter and more cryptic, to the point where some will find it bloodless.
It is as hard to grasp as the cigarette smoke.
Is it possible to be dazzled by the cast, especially by Clive Owen in his Broadway debut, stunned anew by the elusive meanings of Pinter's 'Old Times' and yet appalled by the production?
What should feel haunting, upsetting, frightening and menacing never quite does.
Despite overdetermined design and asymmetrical performances, Pinter's precise, lyrical language comes through with crystalized, cutting force.
But with neither the history nor the hostility very mysterious, the sum on this one-plus-one-plus-one plot is zero.
Transplanting the delicate weirdness of 'Old Times' to Broadway seems absurdist in all the wrong ways.
It is, however, almost perfectly awful, and I think it's safe to say that the fault belongs to Douglas Hodge, the director.
It's a disappointment to say that on my first viewing, it feels like a flawed work that has not dated well.
That's a big part of the fun — if it's possible to find 'fun' in a play this dark.

The result is an electrifying hour of theater that crackles like lightning as Owen, Best, and Reilly ruminate and reminisce on what may or may not be old times together when they were all young and carefree in London 20 years earlier.
This beautiful and bewildering production holds us enthralled from beginning to end.

To borrow a great line from Harold Pinter's Homecoming: 'You never heard such silence,' and in this brilliant Broadway production of Pinter's Old Times, directed by Douglas Hodge, the silences are simply deafening.
Pinter purists will hate this production.
You’re not likely ever to see this play more beautifully done than here and now.
The three performances are perfectly pitched, with Owen's Deeley a convincing mix of bluff bonhomie and underlying menace.
Old Times is just as slippery, mysterious and seductive.
All appear to have their work cut out competing with this production's overwhelming aural and visual effects.

In the new Roundabout Theatre Company production, which opened Tuesday at the Theatre, director Douglas Hodge and a cast that includes Broadway newbie Clive Owen bring a darkly hypnotic pull to the challenging material.
"Old Times" is likely to feel like either an intense roller coaster rush or a dull, nonsensical sketch.
In the end, you're somehow satisfied though you don't know exactly what you've eaten.
That Owens, Best and Reilly do very little to deserve this adulation is somehow beside the point.

But there’s no getting around Pinter’s deliberately cryptic text, and several of Hodge’s choices, rather than working to ground the goings-on in some recognizable reality and thus orient the audience, instead seem to revel in the play’s weirdness.
The visual and aural distractions diminish the work.

Unfortunately, director Douglas Hodge, best known in New York for his flamboyant Tony Award-winning performance as Albin in the 2010 revival of La Cage aux Folles but a famed interpreter of Pinter in London, has made this revival provocative for all the wrong reasons.
As you settle into your seat, the revival of Harold Pinter's Old Times envelops you in a sensual haze, a mesmerizing blend of nostalgia and unease that's impossible to resist.
We didn’t know what the play was about 44 years ago when it premiered on Broadway and we still don’t, but people love to debate the possibilities.
In my opinion, offering a 65-minute play at Broadway prices is pushing the limits.
Those who keep up with these 'Times' will be rewarded.

cn.t: Pinter's enigmatic memory play divides critics between those captivated by the stellar performances and those frustrated by the overwrought staging. Owen, Best, and Reilly earn widespread praise, but Hodge's direction is deemed either bold or misguided.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
